meta.title: R8 research studio: how do you show results so people understand their limits? Findings, three charts, a briefing and a public paragraph
meta.note: The three charts are drawn in the page from the course's own data: cf_targets.json (EIA, Electric Power Monthly, Table 6.07.B, 2025 monthly capacity factors) and town_year.json (the course's cleaned and normalized series of SPP's 2025 hourly demand and wind, EIA-930: implausible demand hours and frozen wind readings replaced, each series divided by its 2025 maximum, in thousandths). The briefing and the public paragraph report R6's fictional study; fromR6 holds its numbers, which the test recomputes with R6's model. Text in braces, such as {c90}, is filled from these numbers on the page.

fromR6.about: R6's model (assets/learn/r06-uncertainty-properly.js): 1,000 runs, seed 6, demand added hour by hour unless named; MW rounded to 5. The test recomputes every value.

bins.label: Holds as written
bins.sub: the number, its scope and its conditions are all there

bins.label: Missing its conditions
bins.sub: true in the study, but silent on where, when or under what assumptions

bins.label: Claims more than shown
bins.sub: a cause, a certainty or a verdict the analysis cannot carry

findings.text: The U.S. utility-scale wind fleet's capacity factor was {cfYear}% in 2025 (EIA).
findings.why: A number, the fleet (plants of 1 MW or more), the year and the source: a reader can check it and knows where it stops. [[capacity-factor|Capacity factor]]: output over full-power output.

findings.text: In SPP's 2025 data, the busiest hour of demand began at {peakHour} {peakTZ} on {peakDay}.
findings.why: Place, year, hour with its time zone, and data named; it says when, and claims nothing about why.

findings.text: With central car uptake, the town's 2035 peak is {c10}–{c90} MW in about 8 of 10 model runs.
findings.why: A range, the case it belongs to (central uptake: 15,000 electric cars in 2035) and what the range means. The model's other conditions belong in the next sentence.

findings.text: Wind farms run at about a third of their capacity.
findings.why: Which fleet, which year? True of the U.S. fleet in 2025 ({cfYear}%), but it moved from {cfLo}% to {cfHi}% month to month.
In summer, yes: all {sumDays} June to August days peaked between 12:00 and 18:00. In winter, {winMorn} of {winDays} days peaked before noon (SPP, 2025).

findings.text: Managed charging cuts the 2035 peak by {mHours} MW.
findings.why: Only with fast car uptake, at the [[median|median]], with demand added hour by hour. Adding the separate peaks ignores when charging happens, so it cannot show this effect.
A verdict the data cannot carry. They show a capacity factor that moved between {cfLo}% and {cfHi}% by month, which planners can use.
The data show when the peak came, not why. Heat is likely, but showing a cause needs weather data and a method that separates it.

findings.text: Managed charging will solve the town's peak problem.
findings.why: “Will solve” claims a certainty and a goal the study never set. It shows a cut of about {mHours} MW in one case.

charts.goodTitle: Wind's capacity factor was highest in {monthHi} and lowest in {monthLo}
charts.question: What makes the late-summer dip look so deep?

options.text: The months run in calendar order.
options.why: Calendar order is right for a seasonal pattern; it misleads nothing.

options.text: The axis starts at 20%, so the bars' lengths no longer compare the values.
options.why: On this axis March's bar is {truncRatio} times September's; the values differ by a factor of {realRatio}. Bars show length, so they start at zero.

options.text: It shows the national fleet, not one farm.
options.why: Worth saying on the chart, but it does not deepen the dip.

fixes.label: Name the fleet, the year and the source
Make the title say what the data show

charts.badTitle: Wind output fell {winFall}% in two weeks
charts.goodTitle: SPP's daily wind output swung widely through 2025
charts.question: Why does wind seem to be falling?

options.text: Two weeks were cut from the year, from a windy day to a calm one.
options.why: The window makes a fall look like a trend. Across 2025, days ran from {dLo}% to {dHi}% of the windiest hour.

options.text: Output is shown as a share of the year's windiest hour.
options.why: A fair scale, if the axis says so. It does not create the fall.
True, but the hours would show the same fall. The window creates it.

fixes.label: Mark the two weeks on it
Make the title say what is measured

charts.badTitle: Prairie Town's demand peaks at {avgPeak} MW
charts.goodTitle: The average of 365 days, hour by hour, with the spread across days
charts.partTitle: The average of 365 days, hour by hour
charts.question: Why would planning for this line fail?

options.text: It is drawn in local time.
options.why: Local time is right for a daily pattern; the hours match what people live by.

options.text: The line is too smooth to read.
options.why: Smoothness is the symptom, not the cause: averaging 365 days removed the spread.

options.text: It averages 365 days; the busiest days go far higher.
options.why: On 1 day in 10 the {p90Hour} hour is above {p90Max} MW, and the year's highest hour was {yearPeak} MW, against the average day's {avgPeak}.

fixes.label: Make the title name the line

fields.label: Chart 1, the wind fleet by month
fields.example: In 2025, the U.S. utility-scale wind fleet's monthly capacity factor ranged from {cfLo}% in September to {cfHi}% in March (EIA).

fields.label: Chart 2, SPP's daily wind
fields.example: In SPP's 2025 data, daily wind output ranged from {dLo}% to {dHi}% of the year's windiest hour, averaging {dMean}%; this selected fortnight does not establish a year-long decline.

fields.label: Chart 3, Prairie Town's average day
fields.example: On Prairie Town's 2025 pattern, the average day peaks at {avgPeak} MW at {avgHour}, but on 1 day in 10 the {p90Hour} hour tops {p90Max} MW, and the year's highest hour was {yearPeak} MW.

facts.v: {c10}–{c90} MW with central car uptake (15,000 electric cars), {f10}–{f90} MW with fast uptake (30,000): [[percentile|P10–P90]], about 8 in 10 of 1,000 runs. 450 MW in 2025.

A programme moving most charging after 23:00. With fast uptake, the [[median|median]] falls from {f50} to {fm50} MW when demand is added hour by hour; adding the separate peaks ignores timing and misses this.
Varied in the runs: growth (0.4–1.6% a year), a weather multiplier on background demand (0.96–1.04) and a car's daily energy (7–13 kWh). Fixed: 2025's hourly pattern; cars charging at home.
A new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each 2035 figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, the programme's cost and sign-up. Outcomes outside the ranges remain possible.

fields.label: The decision
fields.hint: What the council is deciding, in its own words.

fields.label: What we found
fields.hint: The result as a range, what the range means, the case it belongs to and the 2025 value for scale.

fields.label: What the programme changes
fields.hint: Its effect on the peak, with the case and the model it holds in.

fields.label: What it depends on
fields.hint: The assumptions a council member could challenge.

fields.label: What it leaves out
fields.hint: What the study cannot say, next to what it can.

fields.label: What would change this advice
fields.hint: The signal that would make the briefing out of date.

example.decision: Whether to fund a managed-charging programme before 2030.
example.finding: In about 8 of 10 illustrative model runs, the 2035 peak is {c10}–{c90} MW with central car uptake and {f10}–{f90} MW with fast uptake, against 450 MW in 2025.
example.programme: With fast uptake the programme lowers the median by about {mHours} MW, when demand is added hour by hour.
example.depends: Growth, the year's weather and a car's daily energy, varied within illustrative ranges; 2025's daily pattern of demand; cars charging at home.
example.leaves: A large new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each 2035 figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, and the programme's cost and sign-up; outcomes outside the ranges remain possible.
example.change: A connection request from a large customer, or car numbers on the fast path, would call for a new forecast.

public.example: Prairie Town uses the most electricity on summer afternoons. We looked at how that busiest hour could change by 2035 as more people drive electric cars. If they spread at a middle pace, about 8 in 10 of our model runs put it between {c10} and {c90} megawatts, compared with 450 in 2025. If they spread fast, the range moves up to {f10} to {f90}, and higher values are possible. With fast growth in car numbers, charging late at night instead of in the early evening lowered the middle estimate by about {mHours} megawatts in our model. These numbers leave out a large new factory or business, which would add more, and we will update them as new car numbers come in.

exemplars.title: Two briefings for the same council
exemplars.task: Brief the city council on the 2035 peak, ahead of its vote on a managed-charging programme.

parts.text: the town's peak will grow to {claim} MW by 2035
parts.note: One number with “will”: no range, no case, no conditions.

parts.text: Managed charging is the solution and should be funded
parts.note: Advice past the evidence: the study measured a peak, not the programme's cost or sign-up.

parts.text: See the attached figures for details
parts.note: A council member cannot act on figures nobody walked them through.
Asserted, not shown; and checking a model does not remove the future's uncertainty.

parts.text: whether to fund a managed-charging programme before 2030
parts.note: Opens with the council's decision, not the method.

parts.text: in about 8 of 10 illustrative model runs, the 2035 peak is {c10}–{c90} MW with central car uptake and {f10}–{f90} MW with fast uptake, against 450 MW in 2025
parts.note: Ranges with the case each belongs to, what a range means, and the 2025 value for scale.

parts.text: with fast uptake it lowers the median by about {mHours} MW, when demand is added hour by hour
parts.note: The effect, with the case and the model condition it rests on.

parts.text: growth, the year's weather and a car's daily energy, varied within illustrative ranges; 2025's daily pattern; cars charging at home
parts.note: The assumptions a member could challenge, with what the runs varied, in plain words.

parts.text: a large new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, the programme's cost; outcomes outside the ranges remain possible
parts.note: The limits beside the result, not at the end.

parts.text: a connection request from a large customer, or car numbers on the fast path
parts.note: Signposts: what would make the advice out of date.

diff.label: Numbers
diff.good: Ranges, each with its case and its meaning

diff.label: Advice
diff.good: What the evidence shows, and what would change it

exemplars.note: Both briefings are illustrative, about R6's fictional study; their numbers come from R6's model.

chartsTable.misled: An axis from 20% made a {realRatio}× difference look {truncRatio}×.
chartsTable.fix: Bars from zero; fleet, year and source named.
chartsTable.finding: Monthly [[capacity-factor|capacity factor]] ranged from {cfLo}% to {cfHi}% in 2025 (U.S. fleet, EIA).

chartsTable.misled: Two weeks chosen from windy to calm looked like a fall of {winFall}%.
chartsTable.fix: The whole year, with the two weeks marked.
chartsTable.finding: Daily output swung between {dLo}% and {dHi}% of the windiest hour through 2025; this selected fortnight does not establish a year-long decline.

chartsTable.misled: An average of 365 days peaked at {avgPeak} MW; no plan can use that alone.
chartsTable.fix: The spread across days, and the year's highest hour.
chartsTable.finding: The average day peaks at {avgPeak} MW; 1 day in 10 tops {p90Max} MW; the highest hour was {yearPeak} MW.

boundary.title: Where the managed-charging finding holds
boundary.lede: The briefing's programme sentence, as a box a council member can read in ten seconds.
holds: demand is added hour by hour on 2025's pattern, and every day's charging follows the same managed profile;
car uptake is fast (30,000 cars in 2035); with central uptake the cut is smaller;
growth, weather and a car's daily energy stay inside the ranges R6 sampled.
leaves: the programme's cost, and how many drivers sign up;
boundary.source: Model: R6's, 1,000 runs, seed 6. Data: SPP's 2025 hourly demand (EIA-930).

rubric.title: Rate your R8 practice against the rubric's Communication line
rubric.lede: The course rubric's own words. Proficient asks for a six-page paper, which the capstone assesses; here, rate only the parts R8 practises.

competences.look: the parts R8 practises (one key figure that passes the checklist, findings with their conditions, limits beside the result, a briefing, and a public summary of at most 150 words).

rubric.note: Your rating stays in this browser and rates R8's practice only. Proficient in full also needs the capstone's six-page paper.

checklist.label: One message
checklist.text: Each figure makes one point, and its title or caption says which.

checklist.label: Honest axes
checklist.text: Units on every axis; bars start at zero; any zoom is labelled.

checklist.label: The whole picture
checklist.text: The time window and any selection said; the context shown or one click away.

checklist.label: Spread, not only averages
checklist.text: A band or the range beside any average, and what the band means.

checklist.label: Findings with conditions
checklist.text: Each finding: a number with its unit, the place, the time and the main assumption.

checklist.label: Limits beside results
checklist.text: What the study leaves out, next to what it found, not at the end.

checklist.label: The decision first
checklist.text: A briefing opens with the reader's decision and ends with what would change the advice.

checklist.label: A public version
checklist.text: Plain words, at most 150, read back to you by someone outside the field.

checklist.label: Not colour alone
checklist.text: Colour-blind-safe colours, with labels or patterns that carry the meaning too.
